newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore arrives in China to boost ties, scandal lurks.
newsitem.headline: Gore arrives in China to boost ties, scandal lurks.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore arrived in China on Monday for talks aimed at rebuilding the battered Sino-U.S. relationship, but his trip seemed likely to be dogged by scandal over alleged Chinese political donations.

"I have travelled here to reaffirm the vital importance of relations between our nations, and to continue building a lasting peace between China and the United States," Gore said in an arrival statement.

The vice president stepped off Air Force Two to become the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit China since President George Bush in 1989 -- just months before Chinese troops crushed pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.
He had earlier wrapped up a visit to Japan that eased concern in both Washington and Tokyo about cutbacks in U.S. military forces in Asia.

Gore's meetings with Beijing leaders are aimed at strengthening a recent Sino-U.S. rapprochement, but his talks appeared likely to be darkened by a scandal over alleged Chinese funding of U.S. Democratic Party politicians.
Controversy over political funding has already cast a cloud over the four-day visit, which aims to heal ties damaged by disputes ranging from human rights to trade and Taiwan.

The Washington Post has reported that the Federal Bureau of Investigation warned six members of Congress last year that they had been targeted by China to receive illegal campaign contributions from foreign corporations.
Gore has said he will raise the issue during his official talks in Beijing.
In an apparent sign of concern that the political funding issue could obstruct better relations, China sternly denied it had sought to influence U.S. policy through political funding.
"The Chinese government is not involved in the so-called 'political contributions scandal' in the slightest way and is entirely free of guilt," the official People's Daily said.
After talks earlier in the day in Tokyo with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Gore said he would tell Beijing leaders of U.S. concerns about China's treatment of dissidents.

"I will of course discuss human rights with the leadership of China," Gore said. "Nor will it be a surprise to them to have these matters raised... These issues are important to us as Americans because of who we are."
A U.S.-based human rights group said the sister of China's most prominent dissident Wei Jingsheng had appealed to Gore to ask Beijing to free him from a 14-year jail term.

Human rights remain one of the thorniest Sino-U.S. issues, but U.S. officials said sensitive subjects such as China's trade surplus, its bid to join the World Trade Organisation and renewal of its trading status would all be discussed.
Great powers should work together for cooperation and communication within and among nations, Gore said, citing the poem "On Stork Tower" by classical Chinese poet Wang Zhihuan.

"To see the currents of greatest confluence, we must continue climbing the steps of Stork Tower," he said. "That is why I am here. And that is why our two presidents will themselves ascend the tower in the coming months."
Chinese President Jiang Zemin and U.S. President Bill Clinton are expected to exchange visits in the next two years.
While China was the main focus of Gore's East Asia trip, his talks with Tokyo officials helped clear away lingering worries about Japan's future as home to the main U.S. military base in Asia.

Gore was forthright in stating that Washington wanted to maintain present troop levels in Japan and the rest of Asia, while Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was equally vocal in his opposition to groups that want U.S. bases in Japan shut.

During his 24 hours in Japan, part of an Asian tour that also includes South Korea, Gore also delivered a speech to an environmental conference in which he called for international agreement to help cut greenhouse gas emissions.
